book_title: The ₹100 Unit Economics & Why Negative Operating Cash Flow Is a Feature, Not a Bug
question: How does every ₹100 of Groww's FY26 revenue convert into ₹44.84 of net profit—and why did operating cash flow print negative ₹21 crore?

epigraph.quote: In lending and margin-funded brokerage, working capital is not inventory gathering dust; it is the earning asset itself.
epigraph.author: Fintech Cash-Flow Forensics Rule

web_blocks.html: Groww's distribution architecture is built on zero-branch, organic digital pull. Unlike full-service brokers (ICICI Direct, HDFC Securities) or sub-broker-heavy challengers (Angel One), Groww relies overwhelmingly on direct app downloads, word-of-mouth referrals, and financial education content rather than paid physical branch networks or revenue-sharing authorized persons [1, 4]. Once a user onboards via a free direct mutual fund SIP or IPO application, incremental cross-sell into equities, F&O, MTF, and wealth incurs virtually zero marginal customer acquisition cost (CAC).

web_blocks.title: FY26 Per-₹100 Revenue Waterfall & Cost Anatomy

web_blocks.html: In FY26 (year ended March 2026), Groww generated ₹4,645 crore in consolidated revenue from operations [1]. Because it is a software-delivered financial platform with no physical cost of goods sold (COGS = ₹0), gross margin is effectively 100% before operating expenses. Total operating expenses stood at ₹1,901 crore—comprising ₹591 crore in employee benefit expenses (₹5,908.33 million per statutory filings, including BGV ESOS 2024 share-based payments, salaries, allowances, and staff welfare [9]) and ₹1,310 crore in technology, cloud infrastructure, marketing, exchange/KYC, and administrative costs [1, 9]. That yielded an Operating EBITDA of ₹2,744 crore (59.07% OPM), which expanded further to 64.5% OPM in Q2 FY27 [1, 3].

web_blocks.title: Decoding the CFO vs. PAT Divergence (-₹962 Cr in FY25; -₹21 Cr in FY26)

web_blocks.html: A critical forensic question for any investor examining Groww is why a business reporting ₹1,824 crore PAT in FY25 and ₹2,083 crore PAT in FY26 generated negative Cash Flow from Operations (-₹962 crore in FY25 and -₹21 crore in FY26) [1]. In an industrial manufacturer, negative CFO alongside rising PAT signals aggressive revenue recognition or uncollected receivables. In a rapidly scaling brokerage-plus-MTF platform, however, the divergence is mechanical [20]:

web_blocks.title: Three Mechanical Drivers of Negative Operating Cash Flow
paragraphs: 1. MTF Loan Book Deployment: Under Ind-AS cash-flow classification, capital deployed into Margin Trading Facility receivables (scaling toward ₹4,351 Cr by Q2 FY27) is booked as an operating working-capital outflow rather than an investing outflow [14, 20].

2. Segregated Client Funds & Exchange Margin Timing: Year-end shifts in client cash balances, exchange clearing deposits, and settlement receivables create large swings in 'Other Assets' (₹7,768 Cr in Mar 2025 -> ₹14,381 Cr in Mar 2026) and 'Other Liabilities' [1, 20].
3. NBFC Credit Scaling: Groww Creditserv's LAMF and retail loan originations similarly consume operating cash as the loan book grows [12].

web_blocks.html: To verify that negative CFO is growth-capital deployment rather than cash burn, look at three cross-checks. First, physical capex was a minuscule ₹12 crore in FY26 (0.26% of revenue) and ₹17 crore in FY25, proving the core software platform is ultra-asset-light [1]. Second, debtor days remain low at 22 days in FY26, and working capital days remain deeply negative at -257 days [1]. Third, borrowings actually fell from ₹610 crore in Mar 2025 to ₹292 crore in Mar 2026 and ₹77 crore by Sep 2026 [1]. Groww is funding its MTF book largely out of retained earnings and equity reserves rather than debt.

A subtle but decisive advantage in Groww's go-to-market engine is its software-first engineering leverage [1][6]. Unlike legacy full-service brokers that maintain hundreds of physical branches and thousands of relationship managers, or hybrid discount brokers that pay 30%–50% brokerage revenue share to authorized-person (AP) networks, Groww's distribution is 100% digital and direct-to-consumer [1][6]. Server, cloud, and engineering costs scale sub-linearly with order volume, which explains how operating margins expanded to 62%–64% once active users crossed the 1-crore threshold.
Digital scale drives this edge. No branch rent. No sub-broker cut. Software handles the load. Cash flows into MTF loans.

book_paragraphs: Let's put Groww's FY26 income statement under a microscope and trace every ₹100 that walked through the digital door.

Start with distribution. Unlike legacy brokerages that maintain hundreds of leased branches or share 30% to 50% of brokerage with local sub-brokers, Groww acquires the vast majority of its users organically through its mobile app, UPI-first onboarding, and word-of-mouth referrals. When you acquire a customer through a free mutual fund SIP and later cross-sell equities, F&O, and margin lending, your marginal acquisition cost approaches zero.

Now trace the ₹4,645 crore of consolidated FY26 revenue—every ₹100 of sales. Groww spent zero rupees on physical cost of goods sold. It doesn't manufacture widgets or hold warehouse inventory. Its first real expense is engineering and product talent: ₹591 crore in employee benefit expenses (roughly ₹12.72 out of every ₹100), which includes salaries, bonuses, and ESOP share-based payments. Its second expense is technology, cloud servers, exchange connectivity, KYC verification, and marketing: ₹1,310 crore, or ₹28.20 per ₹100.

Add those up, and Groww kept ₹59.07 of Operating EBITDA out of every ₹100 it earned in FY26—and by Q2 FY27, operating leverage pushed that margin even higher, to 64.5%. After deducting just ₹1.03 for depreciation, ₹0.99 for interest, adding ₹3.68 of treasury other income, and paying ₹15.89 in corporate taxes, Groww brought ₹44.84 of pure net profit down to the bottom line. Few consumer-facing financial platforms anywhere in the world convert 45 paise of every revenue rupee into after-tax profit.

Now, here is the forensic puzzle that trips up almost everyone who reads Groww's cash-flow statement for the first time. If Groww earned ₹1,824 crore of net profit in FY25 and ₹2,083 crore in FY26, why was its Cash Flow from Operating Activities negative ₹962 crore in FY25 and negative ₹21 crore in FY26?

In a manufacturing company, negative operating cash flow alongside booming profits is a flashing red siren—usually meaning unpaid customer bills or bloated inventory. In a brokerage scaling a Margin Trading Facility (MTF) book, the accounting works differently. When Groww lends ₹4,000+ crore to customers for MTF stock purchases, Ind-AS accounting treats that expanding loan book as an increase in operating working-capital assets, which shows up as a cash outflow inside CFO. Combine that with year-end timing of segregated client margin funds and exchange clearing deposits, and healthy, interest-earning asset growth makes operating cash flow look negative.

How do you verify that this is productive capital deployment and not hidden cash burn? You check three things: physical capex was a tiny ₹12 crore in FY26; total borrowings actually shrank from ₹610 crore in March 2025 to just ₹77 crore by September 2026; and the MTF book itself is earning daily interest while backed by liquid, pledged equity collateral. Still, this creates a discipline you and I must watch: as MTF scales, Groww is gradually becoming a hybrid of an asset-light tollbooth and a balance-sheet lender.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Negative CFO in FY25 (-₹962 Cr) and FY26 (-₹21 Cr) is not an earnings quality red flag—it is the accounting footprint of funding a ₹4,351 Cr MTF book out of equity. The real watchpoint is credit underwriting if equity markets gap down.

book_subsections.title: Why Zero-Branch Digital Distribution Produces 62% Operating Margins
paragraphs: If you compare a traditional Indian brokerage's income statement against Groww's ₹100 revenue-to-free-cash-flow waterfall, the structural difference hits you immediately. Legacy full-service brokers spend 25 to 35 rupees out of every 100 rupees of revenue on branch leases, relationship-manager salaries, and sub-broker commission payouts. Even hybrid discount brokers rely heavily on authorized-person networks that take a recurring cut of every trade.

Groww runs on software and organic trust. Out of every ₹100 of FY26 revenue (₹4,645 crore total), operating expenses consumed just ₹40.93, leaving ₹59.07 in operating EBITDA—and by Q2 FY27, operating margins expanded even further to 64.5 percent. Depreciation and interest together took barely ₹2.02 per ₹100 of revenue because Groww owns minimal physical real estate and carries almost no debt. After ₹3.68 of other income and taxes, ₹44.84 out of every ₹100 of revenue dropped straight to net profit (₹2,083 crore in FY26).

The only reason free cash flow looked flat in FY26 (-₹33 crore) is that Groww chose to plow that cash generation directly into funding its booming ₹4,351 crore MTF loan book rather than letting cash sit idle in low-yield bank deposits. As an owner, you want to see that distinction clearly: Groww is not burning cash to survive; it is deploying cash into secured, interest-earning client margin loans.

book_subsections.title: The Unit-Economics Advantage of Owning the First Mile of Investing
paragraphs: In consumer finance, the company that owns the customer's first financial habit almost always wins the highest lifetime value. Legacy banks used to own that first mile through savings accounts, but their brokerage apps were clunky and riddled with relationship-manager cross-selling of high-fee products. Groww flipped the script by making the direct mutual fund SIP—a product with zero commission—its front door.

Think about the customer acquisition math: if a traditional broker pays ₹2,500 to ₹4,000 in digital ads and affiliate payouts to acquire one active F&O trader, it needs that trader to survive and trade actively for months just to break even. Groww acquires millions of savers organically at near-zero cost, lets them build trust through ₹5,000 monthly mutual fund SIPs for a year or two, and then captures their equity, IPO, and MTF wallets with zero incremental acquisition spend. That is why Groww's operating expenses sit near 41 percent of revenue while peers spend 65 to 75 percent.

book_subsections.title: Technology Reliability as a Hidden Cost of Distribution
paragraphs: Every digital broker learns eventually that software uptime is not merely an engineering metric—it is a regulatory and brand survival requirement. During high-volatility market sessions, such as budget days or sharp index reversals, retail order flow spikes three- to five-fold in minutes. Legacy brokers with patched-together mainframes often suffer login freezes or order-routing delays, sparking social-media backlash and SEBI scrutiny.

Groww's cloud-native architecture and in-house order-management stack allow it to process millions of concurrent orders without paying third-party vendor royalties per trade. Keeping that infrastructure resilient as MTF and commodities volumes double is an ongoing capex and engineering priority, and one reason Groww's ₹11,568 crore equity cushion is so valuable.
